Four: Chapter two. Four words for cost.

Here is a real airline's year. Delta Air Lines spent fifty-seven and a half billion dollars running its airline in 2025, and every block here is one line of its income statement, drawn to size: salaries, fuel, the refinery it owns, landing fees, maintenance, depreciation of the fleet. Now cancel one flight, tomorrow morning, Atlanta to Boston. Which of these costs go away?

Within days, only the costs of flying that flight. The fuel it would have burned, the landing fee at Boston, the snacks, the commission on the tickets. That is about 31 percent of Delta's costs. These are the variable costs: they move with how much you fly. The crew is still paid this month, the aircraft still sits on the ground, the headquarters in Atlanta still has its lights on. Cancel flying for a year, and most of the rest can go too: staff can be let go, contracts ended, maintenance deferred. That reaches about 95 percent. What is left, the depreciation and rent of the fleet, goes away only as the planes are sold or reach the end of their lives.

So fixed and variable are not properties of a cost. They depend on the horizon of the decision. Over a day almost everything is fixed; over ten years almost nothing is. Economists call that the short run and the long run, and they are not lengths of time but the set of things you can still change.

That gives four words, and they sort costs along two different lines. The first line asks whether a cost rises with how much you make. Fuel does: fly twice as far and you buy twice as much. So do landing fees. Those are variable. A year's pilots, the lease on a hangar, do not change with one flight more or less. Those are fixed. The second line asks whether you get the money back if you stop. A fixed cost can still be avoidable: give notice on the hangar and the rent ends. A sunk cost is gone whatever you do: a chip design that is finished, last year's advertising. And a jet already bought sits on the line: it is only partly sunk, because it can be sold, though for less than you paid.

The top right corner is almost empty, and for a reason. A cost that rises with output can be avoided by making less. Every variable cost is avoidable; the interesting decisions are all about the fixed ones.

Sunk costs matter because people find them so hard to ignore. Your company is building a plant. Eight million dollars are spent; two million more will finish it. Since you began, the market has turned, and the finished plant is now worth only five million. Overall the project loses money: ten million in, five million out. Do you finish it? Yes. From here, two million buys something worth five. The eight already spent is gone either way.

Now suppose finishing would cost six million instead. Stop, even though eight million has been poured in, because six more buys only five. Notice that the eight million appeared in neither decision. It is the same whichever way you choose, so it cannot tell you which way to choose. That is all 'ignore sunk costs' means.

The mistake has a name. In 1976 the biologists Richard Dawkins and Tamsin Carlisle called it the Concorde fallacy, after the supersonic airliner that Britain and France kept paying for long after it was clear it would never pay back, partly, the argument went, because so much had already been spent. The rule it breaks is the one this part keeps using: decide on what a choice changes from here on, the money to come, not the money gone.
Full: The cost of one more is only half of a plant's cost. The other half is the plant itself, and what you pay for it per unit depends on how much you use it. Take a new nuclear plant, with the costs the US Energy Information Administration assumes for one built today: eight thousand dollars of construction for every kilowatt of capacity. Pay that off over thirty years at seven percent, add the staff and upkeep, and each kilowatt costs about 829 dollars a year whether it runs or not. The fuel and the running costs add only 9 dollars a megawatt-hour. Run it flat out, as American reactors do, and a megawatt-hour costs about 109 dollars.

Now run it less. At sixty percent of the time, the same yearly bill is spread over fewer hours, and a megawatt-hour costs 167 dollars. At a quarter of the time, 388. At a tenth, nearly a thousand. Nothing about the plant changed. Only how full it was.

Do the same for every kind of plant you could build, and you get a family of curves. Each falls as the plant runs more, because the yearly bill for the plant is spread over more hours. Each flattens out at its cost of one more megawatt-hour: nothing for wind and solar, whose fuel is free, and the price of gas for the gas plants. Run everything nearly all the time, and the cheapest are solar and wind, then combined-cycle gas, with nuclear dearest. Run everything a tenth of the time, and the order changes: the gas peaker, the cheapest machine to build, wins easily, and nuclear is off the top of the chart.

But most plants do not choose how full they are. The rings mark where each kind of plant actually ran in America in 2025. Wind turbines turned out about a third of what they could, solar panels about a quarter, because the wind drops and the sun sets. Reactors ran ninety-one percent of the time. Combined-cycle gas ran about sixty percent, and the peakers only fourteen. At those rates, a new combined-cycle plant's megawatt-hour costs about 46 dollars, wind's 58, solar's 68, a reactor's 113 and a peaker's 124. And yet power companies still build peakers, at the highest cost on this chart. The next chapters will say why: a peaker is not selling the average megawatt-hour. It sells the hours when nothing else is left.

This is the first rule of the cost curve. The more of a business's cost is paid up front, the more it needs to run full, and the more it will do to fill itself: cut prices, take the order below average cost, keep a reactor on through the night. That is true of reactors, of aircraft, of chip factories and of hotel rooms.
Scope: Scale is about making more of one thing. Scope is about making a second thing with what you already have. A Delta flight to Boston carries passengers, who pay for the plane, the fuel and the crew. Under their feet is a hold with room to spare, and Delta fills it with freight: nine hundred million dollars of cargo revenue in 2025, carried mostly in the holds of flights that would have flown anyway. That is an economy of scope: making two things together costs less than making them apart. The plane, the airport slot and the crew are shared.

Scope reaches further than the hold. Delta's frequent flyers collect miles; Delta sells those miles to American Express, which hands them out to people who carry a Delta credit card. In 2025 American Express paid Delta about eight point two billion dollars, under that deal. Delta's operating profit for the whole year was five point eight billion. The two numbers are not like for like: the miles cost Delta seats it gives away. But the network, the brand and the customers that make the miles worth buying are the same ones that fly the planes. That is scope.

Density is scope's cousin: the second customer on the same street. A delivery van drives the same loop every day. The van and the driver cost about a hundred dollars for the loop, however many parcels it carries; each stop adds a minute and a little under two dollars. If one house in twenty orders, the van drives past nineteen doors for every one it stops at, and each parcel costs about 18 dollars to deliver. Fill the street. At one house in five, the cost falls to under 6 dollars; at half the street, about 3.34. The road, the van and the driver are shared over more parcels.

This is why delivery firms, postal services, cable companies and power lines care so much about density, and why a second network on the same street finds it hard to catch the first: with half the customers per mile, every one of them costs more to serve. Density is why the first network on a street is so hard to catch.
Learning: In 1975 a solar module, the panel itself without the frame or the wiring, cost about 132 dollars for every watt it could produce, in today's money. A panel the size of one on a roof today would have cost about forty thousand dollars. Solar power was for satellites. Then, year after year, the price fell. By 2025 a watt cost about 12 cents. The same panel: about thirty-six dollars. The price fell more than a thousandfold.

Plot the price year by year, and you see a cliff, then a floor. But this picture hides almost everything. Every fall after 1990 looks like nothing, because the early prices were so high. Change the vertical scale so that each step up is ten times the last. A fall from a hundred dollars to ten now looks the same as a fall from a dollar to ten cents, and the cliff becomes a steady slope: the price kept falling, by roughly the same share, decade after decade.

Now Wright's idea. Instead of the year, put along the bottom how much solar the world had built so far, again on a scale where each step is ten times the last. Capacity records start in 2000, so the earlier years drop out. The points fall onto a line. Every time the world's solar capacity has doubled, the price of a module has fallen by about 30 percent. From 2000 to 2025 the capacity doubled almost eleven times, and the price fell to about a fiftieth.

That is Wright's aeroplane rule again, fifty years and an industry away. But be careful what it says. It is a pattern in the record, not a law of nature. Some of the fall was learning: thinner wafers, better cells, fewer broken ones. Some was scale: giant factories, most of them in China. Some was subsidy, and some was cheaper silicon. And the arrow runs both ways: building more made panels cheaper, but cheaper panels also made people build more. Still, it is one of the most reliable patterns in industry, and it has a hard edge: whoever has built the most is furthest down the curve, so the leader's costs keep falling faster than a newcomer can follow.
Seats: Airlines are the cleanest case of a business that sells capacity. Once a flight is scheduled, almost all its costs are set: the plane, the crew, the fuel, the landing fee. Delta's costs in 2025 came to 19.3 cents for every seat it flew one mile, full or empty. Its revenue, spread over the seats that were filled, came to about 25 cents a mile, counting everything it earns, from fares to cargo to selling miles. So board the plane. The first passengers pay for the flight itself. Only once about three seats in four are full does the flight break even: at 76 percent. Delta filled 84 percent of its seats. The last few passengers on each flight, the green ones, are the whole profit.

On a plane of 120 seats, that is about 92 passengers to pay for the flight, 9 more who make the profit, and 19 empty seats. Now look at what one more passenger is worth. Across Delta's whole network, one percentage point of load factor, one more seat in a hundred filled, brings in about 0.75 billion dollars a year, and costs almost nothing extra to carry: a meal, a little fuel. Lose eight points, back down to the break-even, and the whole year's operating profit of 5.8 billion is gone. This is a rough sum, since not all of Delta's revenue comes from its passengers, but it is why airlines fight so hard for the last seat, and why that seat is sold at almost any price on the morning of the flight.
Leverage: Fixed costs do something else: they amplify. Take two businesses that each sell a hundred million dollars a year and each make ten million of profit. A hotel, whose building, staff and loans cost seventy million a year whatever happens; each guest adds only twenty cents of cost per dollar, for cleaning and breakfast. And a temp agency, which owns almost nothing: it pays its workers eighty cents of every dollar it bills, and has ten million of fixed costs. Same sales, same profit.

Now a recession takes a fifth off both their sales. The agency sends fewer workers out and pays fewer wages; its profit falls from ten million to six. The hotel's rooms are emptier, but its building costs the same. Its profit falls from ten million to a loss of six. Run it the other way, a boom with a fifth more sales, and the hotel's profit jumps to twenty-six million while the agency's rises to fourteen. Economists call this operating leverage. A one percent change in the hotel's sales moves its profit by eight percent; the agency's by two.

Airlines are hotels with wings, and in 2020 the world ran the experiment. In 2019 Delta took in 47 billion dollars, spent 40 and made an operating profit of 6.6 billion. In 2020 the pandemic emptied its planes. Revenue fell by 64 percent. Costs, as reported, fell by only 27 percent: the planes, the leases, the airports and much of the staff still had to be paid, and the year's costs include the price of retiring planes and people early. A profit of 6.6 billion became a loss of 12.5 billion.

High fixed costs make the good years very good and the bad years very bad. That is why such businesses borrow carefully, hold cash, and fight for every last customer when demand turns, which is the story of the last chapters of this part.
Zero: Now push the cost curve to its limit. The first copy of a piece of software costs years of engineers' work. The second copy costs nothing: copy the file. So does the thousandth, and the millionth. A factory's average cost falls as it fills, then flattens at the cost of one more unit. Software's never flattens. It just keeps falling, towards zero, the more copies are sold.

Microsoft shows what that does to a business. Its office software, Microsoft 365, with LinkedIn and its business applications, sold about a hundred and forty billion dollars in fiscal 2026 and kept about eighty-four billion as operating profit: sixty cents of every dollar. Selling one more subscription costs Microsoft almost nothing. But look at its cloud. Renting out computing power, and above all running artificial intelligence, needs a data centre, electricity and chips for every answer. The cost of one more is no longer zero. The cloud's margin is forty-one percent, and its cost of revenue grew 44 percent in a year, driven, Microsoft says, by its investment in AI infrastructure.

Zero marginal cost changes the rules. A price can no longer be cost plus a markup, because there is no cost to add to: it is set by what buyers will pay. And the company with the most users spreads its fixed cost thinnest, can spend the most on the next version, and pulls further ahead. That is why software markets so often end with one winner, a story this series takes up again when it reaches the platforms.
Called: Every part ends by checking forecasts. This one has a famous pair. In 2010 the International Energy Agency published a roadmap for solar power. It was meant to be ambitious: world capacity could reach two hundred gigawatts by 2020, nine hundred by 2030 and two thousand by 2040. Here is what was built. By 2020 the world had over seven hundred gigawatts, more than three times the roadmap. By 2025, about two thousand four hundred: the roadmap's figure for 2040, fifteen years early.

Why so wrong? Not for lack of expertise. The roadmap assumed costs would fall, but not as fast as they did, and it did not let the falling cost feed back into demand. Each doubling made panels cheaper; cheaper panels sold more; more panels made the next doubling come sooner. Forecasts of solar have erred in the same direction again and again. When an industry rides a learning curve, the safe bet is that the curve keeps going.

And this part's own call, on the record. In at least one month of 2027, America's utility-scale solar farms will generate more electricity than its coal plants. In 2025 coal still made 730 terawatt-hours against solar's 298. The Energy Information Administration expects about forty percent more solar by 2027, as seventy gigawatts of new panels come on line, and less coal. Over the whole of April to June 2027, it expects 126 terawatt-hours of solar against 135 of coal: close. Spring is when the sun climbs and coal plants close for maintenance, so a single month, April or May, could tip. We put it at fifty-five percent, a little better than a coin toss, and it will be scored on the final 2027 figures.
